findings.text: Early boot builds the initial mount world by creating a base null style mount and a mutable root style mount, placing the second over the first, registering the connected tree in the initial namespace, then creating isolated kernel thread mounts and pointing the initial task root and working location at the private mount while attaching the namespace.

Early subsystem preparation initializes a fixed size array of node guards, initializes a device keyed superblock table, and creates a kernfs hierarchy root plus filesystem registration for the system view, destroying the fresh root if registration fails.

Filesystem context root and current location replacement takes a new reference on the incoming location, swaps the stored location under exclusive sequence protection, releases the prior location when present, and leaves reference handling safe against concurrent readers of the sequence guarded fields.
Mount namespace handle acquisition increments the namespace reference count through a small inline helper, used during boot when assigning the initial namespace to the initial task.

Kernfs hierarchy root creation allocates and initializes identifier tracking, hierarchy and attribute and superblock guards, super list, rename guard, identity high portion, callback table, flags, embedded directory node and wait queue, then optionally activates the tree; destruction removes the root node and drops references so the root itself is eventually freed.

Kernfs node reference handling ignores null input, warns if incrementing from zero, and on last decrement reclaims symlink targets, extended attribute state and identifier allocation before deferred freeing, then walks upward releasing ancestors until a live ancestor remains or the root itself is destroyed.

Public hierarchy activation and removal operate on whole subtrees under hierarchy exclusion, with removal additionally excluding superblock changes; removal is null tolerant while activation assumes a valid starting node and both delegate per node work to internal helpers.

Boot mount topology expects the base mount to carry the first identifier and the mutable root the second, keeps the namespace root on the base mount, marks the kernel thread root unmountable and read only, and builds a second private mount rooted on a regular stand in file with internal marking and writable state plus unmountable root.

Kernfs identity combines a high portion kept in the root with a cyclic low portion from an allocator starting at one; on wide inode number builds the full identity serves as the inode number while on narrow builds only the low half does, with wrap detected by comparing against the previous low value to bump the high portion.

A newborn node starts with a single reference, a deactivated bias in its active counter, cleared tree linkage, duplicated name, supplied mode and type flags, optional non root ownership materialized through attribute storage, and when a parent exists a held parent reference plus security initialization, with ordered cleanup of parent link and attributes and identity and cache on failure.

Node kind is derived by masking stored flags with a type mask and inode number is derived from the stored 64 bit identity with width dependent truncation; an alternate build configuration provides a degenerate kind query that always reports zero.

Attribute assignment only touches fields selected by a validity mask, directing ownership and timestamps into auxiliary attribute storage while directing mode into the node itself, allocating auxiliary storage on demand and reporting resource exhaustion when allocation fails.

Descendant iteration proceeds in postorder using leftmost descent into directory children linked in an ordered tree, then next sibling subtrees, then the parent, terminating after the starting node itself, and requires exclusive hierarchy ownership throughout.

Sibling detachment succeeds exactly once per node as judged by tree linkage state, decrementing the parent directory count for directories and bumping a parent revision counter under attribute exclusion before erasing tree linkage and marking it cleared.

Extended attribute teardown repeatedly removes the first list entry from a hash index and list accounting, optionally accumulating reclaimed space, then frees each entry by deferred reclamation; cache destruction warns if entries remain, tears down the hash table, and clears the owning pointer.

Filesystem root and working directory updates serialize writers with an exclusive sequence guard while taking the new reference before the critical section and releasing the old reference after it, allowing lock free readers to retry on concurrent modification.

Hierarchy mutation requires exclusive ownership of the root hierarchy guard, with full removal additionally requiring shared ownership of the superblock guard; attribute mass marking and parent timestamp and link maintenance use the attribute guard, and draining temporarily releases hierarchy and optionally superblock guards while waiting then reacquires them in reverse order.

Identifier allocation and release serialize on a root spin style guard with preload management around cyclic allocation, while per node open file state serializes on a hashed mutex selected from a fixed pool by hashing the node address, with protected dereference asserting that the same hashed guard is held.

The cached parent pointer is only stable under hierarchy exclusion or rename exclusion or while the node reference count is already zero, and helpers expose whether the current context holds the hierarchy guard or the rename guard for the root owning a given node.

A kernfs hierarchy root bundles cyclic identifier state with high and low tracking plus its guard, separate guards for hierarchy shape versus attribute data versus superblock membership, a superblock list, a rename guard, a revisioned directory node for the top, callback operations and creation flags, a deactivation wait queue, and an extended attribute cache with deferred freeing support.

A kernfs node bundles a wide identity, reference and active counters, ordered tree linkage, reference counted name, mode and type and lifecycle flags, a parent pointer, optional auxiliary attributes with timestamps and ownership and extended attributes, directory child linkage with counts and revision, symlink target linkage, open file state, optional lock validation state, and deferred reclamation linkage.

Nodes begin deactivated with a negative bias; activation marks every descendant as activated then clears the bias exactly once for nodes that are neither already active nor hidden nor being removed, leaving hidden or removing nodes biased until a later path handles them.

Removal first flags the whole target subtree as removing and moves active nodes back to biased form, then repeatedly drains the leftmost remaining descendant while holding a temporary reference, unlinks each drained node once with parent link and timestamp maintenance, and stops after the original target itself has been processed.

Open file draining is needed only when shared open state exists with mapped or release pending counts; the drain pass unmaps mapped files and clears their mapped indication while invoking release handling for nodes that request it, expecting both pending counts to reach zero before the guard is released.

Boot mount setup treats failures to create base or mutable or private mounts or the file rooted stand in, and failure to lock the mount point for stacking, as fatal, as is failure to initialize the device keyed superblock table.

Misuse diagnostics cover incrementing a zero reference count, releasing a node whose active counter is not at the biased rest value, draining an active node, activating a linked child without proper bias, leaving mapped or release pending opens after draining, and destroying a non empty attribute cache.

Extended attribute space accounting uses a fixed architecture independent base of forty plus payload size plus name length, deliberately independent of the in memory descriptor size so results match across word sizes and future growth.

The null style regular stand in file uses inode number two with the root directory understood as number one, regular file kind with widely writable permissions, dedicated file operation tables, synchronized timestamps, and suppression of access time updates.
